title: Linear Regression From Scratch
scope: Build, train, and evaluate a one-feature linear-regression model using only arithmetic and gradient descent.
beginnerEntry: You understand features and targets, linear functions, mean squared error, derivatives, and parameter updates.

knowledge.history: Galton noticed 'regression to the mean' in heredity data in 1886, using the least-squares machinery Legendre and Gauss built for astronomy. Linear regression became the first supervised learning algorithm — and its predict → measure loss → gradient step loop is, unchanged, the loop that trains GPT.

mentalModels.name: Best straight line through experience
mentalModels.description: The model is one line summarizing every (input, outcome) pair seen so far. Prediction is reading the line; training is choosing the line that disagrees least with experience.

mentalModels.name: The learning loop
mentalModels.description: Predict with current parameters, measure the error, nudge the parameters downhill, repeat. Every learning system from this lesson to a frontier LLM runs this exact loop at different scale.

analogies.analogy: A pricing rule of thumb refined after every sale
analogies.whenToUse: When framing training as experience gradually adjusting a simple rule.

analogies.analogy: Tuning a shower knob toward comfortable by feel
analogies.whenToUse: When connecting gradient steps to small corrective adjustments.

objectives: Compute mean squared error for a dataset.
Derive and apply gradients for w and b.
Implement and evaluate training without an ML library.

steps.prompt: Study pairs (hours, score): (1,2), (2,4), (3,6). Describe the simplest rule, then identify what slope and intercept mean in this context.
When real points do not lie on one exact line, how can a machine choose w and b rather than guessing them?
Start w = 0, b = 0. For x = 2, y = 4, predict y-hat, error, squared loss, and whether w should increase or decrease.

Play the fit-line experiment above: first minimize the MSE by hand with the sliders, then reset and let gradient steps do it. Which approach found a lower error, and which scales to a million parameters?
Break it: set w and b as badly as possible and note the MSE. Then take gradient steps from there. Why does the same update rule recover from any starting point on this loss surface?
State your discovery: training is not magic — it is measuring squared error and repeatedly applying dw = mean(2x(ŷ−y)), db = mean(2(ŷ−y)). You have now trained a model from scratch.
Linear regression predicts y-hat = wx + b, averages squared errors, and updates w and b opposite their loss gradients. Repeating this loop fits a line to training evidence.

By hand, run one full training step on (2, 4) and (3, 5) starting from w = 0, b = 0 with learning rate 0.1: predict both y-hats, compute both errors and the MSE, compute dw = mean(2x(y-hat - y)) and db = mean(2(y-hat - y)), and update w and b. Say aloud what just improved.

Every idea in this path is now on the table at once: numbers with units in each cell, features as vectors, the dataset as a matrix, error statistics, gradients for direction, and a loss to descend. Linear regression is where they assemble into one working machine.

After hundreds of update loops the line stops moving. How would you convince a skeptic the machine actually learned something, rather than memorized its training rows? What role do the held-out test rows play?

A line fits training data with low MSE. Predict what happens to test error when the true relationship curves, when one outlier row is corrupted, and when the model predicts far outside the range of x it ever saw.

Evaluation completes the loop: report MSE on unseen test rows, inspect residuals for leftover pattern, and refuse to extrapolate blindly. A fitted slope shows association, not causation. Every serious ML system, however large, still follows this predict-score-update-evaluate cycle.

Write from-scratch pseudocode: initialize w,b; loop over epochs; predict each y-hat; accumulate MSE gradients dw = mean(2x(y-hat-y)) and db = mean(2(y-hat-y)); update parameters; report test MSE and one residual limitation. You have built machine learning from raw numbers. The straight line is also your first wall: real patterns curve, and models that learn curves, neural networks, are the story's next chapter.

experiments.title: Train a model with your own hands
experiments.instructions: Slide w and b to lower the MSE yourself, then press the gradient-step button and watch the exact update rule dw = mean(2x(ŷ−y)), db = mean(2(ŷ−y)) do your job automatically.

measurement.prePrompt: Describe how a line could make numeric predictions and how its parameters might improve from mistakes.
measurement.postPrompt: For a three-row dataset, calculate predictions and MSE, derive dw and db, perform one update, write the full training loop without an ML library, and explain test evaluation and limitations.
successCriteria: Defines feature, target, slope, and intercept.
Computes predictions and mean squared error.
Derives or correctly applies both gradients.
Provides a complete from-scratch loop and evaluates unseen data.

checks.label: Describe the linear model with slope and intercept.
Reference the loss such as mean squared error.
Describe training as iterative gradient updates.
Reason about evaluation on unseen data.
Connect regression to prediction or a baseline in production.

misconceptions: Linear regression requires a library to be machine learning.
The best line must pass through every point.
Lower training loss guarantees useful predictions.
Correlation or fitted slope proves causation.
reasoning.tutorGuidance: Trace one row through predict, compare, square, differentiate, and update. Keep w and b meanings visible. Require a held-out check and discussion of linearity, outliers, extrapolation, and non-causal interpretation.
